pedagogy.summary: Pythagoras' Theorem (a²+b²=c²) lets pupils find an unknown side of a right-angled triangle. Experts see one step; novices experience many (Barton): identify the hypotenuse, decide whether Pythagoras applies, recall the relationship, decide square-and-ADD (finding the hypotenuse) vs square-and-SUBTRACT (finding a shorter side), substitute, and take the square root. The load-bearing obstacle is identifying the hypotenuse by POSITION (opposite the right angle, always the longest side) rather than by its number — and then letting that identification choose the operation. A side is the hypotenuse because it is opposite the right angle, not because of the digits on it (Foster).
bestPractices: Label the hypotenuse FIRST, before any calculation, using its two-part identity: opposite the right angle AND the longest side — then let that decide add vs subtract
Vary triangle orientation deliberately and use non-examples: pupils circle the hypotenuse across triangles rotated every which way so they don't default to 'the missing side is always c'
Contrast tasks where the SAME numeric length is a leg in one triangle and the hypotenuse in another (Foster), breaking the habit of judging by the number
Separate the two question types explicitly — 'find the hypotenuse' (square and add) vs 'find a shorter side' (square and subtract) — and practise switching between them
Build in a reasonableness check tied to the hypotenuse's identity: the hypotenuse must be the longest side, so a hypotenuse of 25 for legs 3 and 4 is impossible
For coordinate distance, draw the horizontal and vertical legs explicitly so the segment between the points is seen as the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle
keyRepresentations: The three squares on the three sides — the two smaller squares' areas summing to the largest (area-dissection proof)
A right-angled triangle with the hypotenuse circled (opposite the right angle) before any numbers are used
Coordinate grid with the horizontal and vertical legs drawn between two points and the connecting segment as the hypotenuse
Side-by-side triangles where one shared length is a leg in one and a hypotenuse in the other
commonMisconceptions: Assumes the unknown side is always the hypotenuse, so always squares and ADDS — even when asked for a shorter side (the most common error; often triggered by triangle orientation)
Muddles a hypotenuse with a leg — judges by the number rather than by which side is opposite the right angle
When finding a shorter side, subtracts the wrong way around (leg² − hypotenuse² instead of hypotenuse² − leg²)
Forgets the final square root, reporting the squared value (e.g. 25 instead of 5)
For coordinate distance, adds the horizontal and vertical differences (3+4=7) or counts diagonal grid squares instead of forming a right triangle and applying the theorem

learn.summary: Teaches pupils to apply Pythagoras' Theorem (a²+b²=c²) to find an unknown side of a right-angled triangle, including on a coordinate grid. The load-bearing move is identifying the hypotenuse by POSITION (opposite the right angle, always the longest side) — not by its digits — and then letting whether the hypotenuse is known or unknown decide square-and-ADD (finding the hypotenuse) vs square-and-SUBTRACT, hypotenuse²−leg² (finding a shorter side). Experts see one step; novices experience many: identify the hypotenuse, decide whether Pythagoras applies, recall the relationship, choose add vs subtract, substitute, and take the square root.

activities.title: Pour the squares: seeing a²+b²=c²
feedback: If the two smaller squares exactly tile the largest, confirm: 'The areas on the two shorter sides add up to the area on the longest side — that is a²+b²=c².'
As the legs are dragged, keep the live readout visible so pupils see the relationship hold for every triangle, not just one.
Reinforce that the largest square always sits on the side opposite the right angle (the hypotenuse).
activities.rationale: Grounding the symbolic relationship in an area-dissection the pupil can recompute makes a²+b²=c² meaningful before it is used procedurally. Live recomputation (dragging legs, pouring tiles, updating readout) lets the relationship be seen as true rather than told.
learnerActions: Drag the two legs of a right-angled triangle and watch a square inflate on each of the three sides.
Watch the two smaller squares dissolve and tile, piece by piece, into the big square on the longest side, filling it exactly.
Read a live readout that updates to show a²+b²=c² as the legs change.
Optionally tap each square to reveal its area and confirm the two smaller areas sum to the largest.
activities.intendedInsight: The theorem is a relationship between the areas of the squares on the three sides: the two smaller squares together exactly fill the square on the hypotenuse, so a²+b² IS c² rather than a formula to memorise.

activities.title: Circle the hypotenuse first, then choose add or subtract
feedback: If a pupil picks 'add' for a shorter-side question, show the square built on their computed leg visibly overflow the hypotenuse square to force the rethink, then prompt: 'If this is bigger than the hypotenuse, something is wrong — the hypotenuse must be the longest side.'
If the hypotenuse is misidentified on a rotated triangle, point back to the right angle: 'The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle — find the right angle first.'

If a pupil subtracts leg²−hypotenuse² and gets a negative/nonsense value, anchor on the identity: the hypotenuse's square is the TOTAL, so a missing leg is hypotenuse²−leg² (rearranging c²=a²+b² to a²=c²−b²).

If a pupil reports the squared value as the length (e.g. 144 for a triangle with hypotenuse 13 and leg 5, since 13²−5²=144), prompt the last step and reasonableness: '144 is larger than the hypotenuse 13, so it cannot be a shorter side — take the square root to get the length (√144 = 12).'
On the paired-triangle task, confirm: 'The 10 is a hypotenuse here because it is opposite the right angle, and a leg there — the number alone does not decide.'
activities.rationale: The most common error is reflexively squaring-and-adding for every triangle, often triggered by orientation; forcing hypotenuse identification by position before the operation unlocks, and contrasting triangles where the same number plays different roles, directly targets both the always-add error and judging by digits. Separating 'find the hypotenuse' from 'find a shorter side' makes the add-vs-subtract decision explicit, and a longest-side reasonableness check catches add-when-should-subtract and the missing square root.
sourceClaims: On a diagnostic item asking for a SHORTER side, the most popular wrong answer came from pupils who failed to realise they were not being asked for the hypotenuse and applied a²+b²=c² by adding the two given sides (attributed partly to triangle orientation); another wrong answer subtracted the wrong way around (smaller minus larger); another had the correct subtraction but forgot to take the square root. Pythagoras is a multi-step process for novices: identify the hypotenuse, decide if Pythagoras applies, recall the formula, rearrange, substitute, calculate, interpret.

Pupils often muddle up calculating a hypotenuse with calculating a leg; the same numeric length can be a leg in one triangle and a hypotenuse in another, so a side is the hypotenuse because it is opposite the right angle, not because of its number (a 10 cm side must be the hypotenuse because it is opposite the right angle). Teachers should watch for pupils being unsure whether to square-and-add or square-and-subtract, which depends on whether the unknown is the hypotenuse or a leg.
learnerActions: On right-angled triangles drawn in varied orientations (none with the right angle at the bottom-left), tap or circle the hypotenuse — accepted only when it is the side opposite the right angle, not the longest-looking one on the page.
For each triangle, state whether the hypotenuse is the KNOWN side or the UNKNOWN side before choosing an operation.
Choose square-and-ADD when the unknown side is the hypotenuse; choose square-and-SUBTRACT (hypotenuse²−leg²) when the unknown is a shorter side.
Compare two side-by-side triangles where the same numeric length (e.g. 10) is a leg in one and the hypotenuse in the other, and label each correctly.
Finish each calculation by taking the square root, then check the hypotenuse is the longest side.
activities.intendedInsight: A side is the hypotenuse because it is opposite the right angle (and so the longest), not because of its digits; which side is unknown — not the size of the numbers — decides whether you add or subtract.

activities.title: Distance between two points as a hypotenuse
feedback: If a pupil adds the differences (e.g. 4+3=7), prompt: 'Adding the two leg lengths does not give the hypotenuse — square each, add, then take the square root: √(4²+3²)=√25=5.'
If a pupil counts diagonal grid squares along the sloping line, redraw the horizontal and vertical legs and return to the right-triangle picture.
Confirm the method transfers: 'You built the right triangle from the coordinate differences — the same move works for any two points.'
activities.rationale: Coordinate distance is a real-world/geometry application, and the characteristic errors (adding differences, counting diagonal squares) come from not forming a right triangle. Drawing the legs explicitly between draggable points keeps it as a Pythagoras problem rather than a new formula to memorise.
learnerActions: Plot two points on a coordinate grid (e.g. (1,2) and (5,5)).
Draw the horizontal and vertical legs between the points explicitly, so the connecting segment is seen as the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle.
Find the horizontal difference (Δx) and vertical difference (Δy), then compute distance = √(Δx²+Δy²).
Try a second pair of points unprompted, constructing the right triangle yourself before calculating.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding the straight-line distance between two points is a Pythagoras problem: the segment between them is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the horizontal and vertical differences.

constraints: Pupils must identify the hypotenuse by position (opposite the right angle) before choosing an operation; do not let the activity accept the longest-looking side on the page or let the add/subtract choice precede this identification.
Vary triangle orientation deliberately, including right angles not at the bottom-left, so pupils do not default to 'the missing side is always c'.
Every calculation must end with a square root and a longest-side reasonableness check (a shorter side cannot exceed the hypotenuse), to catch the un-rooted value and add-when-should-subtract errors.

A static tap-to-reveal card can present the area-square proof and the two-part hypotenuse identity, but it cannot recompute as the triangle changes, so the add-vs-subtract decision stays told rather than practised — treat it as a summary scaffold, not the main task.

A recognition-only quiz (which side is the hypotenuse? add or subtract? fill the blank, plus a coordinate item with a 4+3=7 distractor) can reliably score the method-choice in fixed steps, but does not itself let the pupil see the leg-squares fill the hypotenuse square or construct the right triangle themselves.

A spoken/in-role character can pose problems verbally but does not itself render the area relationship or the coordinate legs the pupil must produce and see; keep the discriminating evidence as a computed length and a correctly identified hypotenuse.
3D space-diagonal work (√(a²+b²+c²)) is a later extension beyond this topic's add-vs-subtract objective; reserve it rather than including it here.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the teaching principle, not the efficacy of any specific activity.

Self-audit of worked values (all consistent with the source): √(6²+8²)=√100=10; √(13²−5²)=√144=12; √(4²+3²)=√25=5 for the (1,2)→(5,5) distance (Δx=4, Δy=3). These check out and were kept in feedback/examples.

The source claim that '3D adds nothing to the core insight' is a catalog-style comparison; it has been softened to a scoped statement that 3D space-diagonals are a later extension beyond this topic, not a universal claim about 3D's value.

Claims that a static image 'cannot practise' the decision and that a conversation 'cannot render' the relationship were softened to narrowly-scoped affordance/limit statements in constraints rather than asserted as universal laws.

The National Curriculum coordinate-grid claim is marked verified:false in the source row; it establishes that coordinate-grid Pythagoras is in KS3 scope but does not support the specific teaching principle of the coordinate activity, so it is retained here as scope context rather than cited as a sourceClaim.

In any right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is strictly the longest side, so 'opposite the right angle' and 'longest side' never conflict, including near-isosceles cases; flagged only for reviewer awareness.

probeDeeper: 'Show me the hypotenuse on this one' — then rotate the triangle 130° and ask again; does the pupil track it by position (opposite the right angle) or lose it?

Counterexample: 'Here is a triangle with sides 5, 12 and 13. If I tell you the answer for the missing side came out bigger than 13, what has gone wrong?' (the hypotenuse must be the longest — flushes out add-when-should-subtract).
'You added for triangle A and subtracted for triangle B — how did each triangle tell you which to do?' (checks the decision is driven by which side is unknown, not guessed).
'Without a triangle drawn, find the distance from (2,1) to (7,13). What right-angled triangle are you using?' (checks they can construct the legs from coordinates themselves).
assess.correctAnswer: (1) The hypotenuse is circled as the side opposite the right angle on every triangle, regardless of orientation. (2) √(6²+8²)=√100=10 cm (square and add — finding the hypotenuse). (3) √(13²−5²)=√144=12 cm (square and subtract — finding a shorter side, hypotenuse² minus leg²). (4) Horizontal leg 4, vertical leg 3, distance √(4²+3²)=√25=5 (forms a right triangle from the coordinate differences).

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes the unknown is always the hypotenuse, so squares and ADDS every time: 'a²+b²=c², so I add the two numbers' — even when asked for a shorter side
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the pupil circle the hypotenuse FIRST (opposite the right angle, longest side) and state whether it is known or unknown before choosing the operation: unknown hypotenuse → add; unknown leg → subtract. Contrast triangles where the same length is a leg in one and the hypotenuse in another. Reteach right-angle/triangle-property identification.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 3 adds 13²+5² and roots (≈13.9) instead of subtracting; may misidentify the hypotenuse on the rotated triangles in task 1; the orientation of the triangle often triggers the default

errorPatterns.pattern: Subtracts the wrong way around when finding a shorter side: computes leg² − hypotenuse² (smaller minus larger) because 'it's the smaller side so put the smaller number first'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor on the identity a²+b²=c²: the hypotenuse is the largest, so its square is the TOTAL; a missing leg is total minus the other leg's square, hypotenuse² − leg². Rearranging c²=a²+b² to a²=c²−b² is the formula move to reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 3 writes 5²−13² and gets a negative or nonsense value; the operation type (subtract) is right but the order is reversed

errorPatterns.pattern: Forgets the final square root, reporting the squared value as the length (e.g. gives 100 or 144 instead of 10 or 12)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: add a routine last step and a reasonableness check — the hypotenuse must be the longest side, so 144 for these lengths is impossible; the answer must be re-rooted. Have the pupil sketch and sanity-check magnitude.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes the correct squared expression (13²−5²=144) then stops, or gives the un-rooted number as the answer

errorPatterns.pattern: For coordinate distance, adds the horizontal and vertical differences (4+3=7) or counts diagonal grid squares instead of forming a right triangle and applying the theorem
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach in place: draw the horizontal and vertical legs between the two points explicitly; the connecting segment is the hypotenuse, so distance = √(Δx²+Δy²). Return to the right-triangle picture rather than treating it as a new formula.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 4 gives 7, or counts squares along the sloping line; does not draw the horizontal and vertical legs

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably identify the hypotenuse once the triangle is rotated; squares and adds on every task, including the shorter-side question; or adds coordinate differences. Treats a²+b²=c² as 'add the two numbers'.
responseLevels.full: Identifies the hypotenuse by position in any orientation; chooses square-and-add for an unknown hypotenuse and square-and-subtract (hypotenuse² − leg², correct order) for an unknown leg; square-roots and sanity-checks that the hypotenuse is longest; and constructs a right triangle from coordinate differences to find distance, transferring the method to a new pair unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Finds the hypotenuse correctly and squares-and-adds (task 2), but stumbles on the shorter-side case — subtracts the wrong way, reverts to adding, or omits the square root — or cannot form the right triangle for the coordinate distance. Lists the steps but does not let 'which side is unknown' govern add vs subtract.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the pupil three right-angled triangles drawn in DIFFERENT orientations (none with the right angle at the bottom-left) plus a coordinate grid, and set four tasks to WATCH them do — do not explain first: (1) On each triangle, circle the hypotenuse. (2) Triangle A has the two shorter sides 6 cm and 8 cm — find the third side. (3) Triangle B has hypotenuse 13 cm and one shorter side 5 cm — find the other shorter side. (4) Plot the points (1,2) and (5,5) and find the straight-line distance between them. Watch how they identify the hypotenuse, whether they add or subtract, and whether they finish with a square root.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The set forces the discriminating decisions the theorem depends on. Varied orientation exposes whoever identifies the hypotenuse by look or position-on-the-page rather than 'opposite the right angle'. Task 3 (a shorter-side question) separates pupils who square-and-subtract from those who reflexively square-and-add for every triangle. Task 4 separates pupils who form a right triangle from the coordinate differences from those who add the differences or count diagonal squares. A pupil who mechanically adds and roots will succeed on 2 but fail 3 — the tell.
